source: Pinon & Gambara (2005) A meta-analytic review of framing effect: risky, attribute and goal framing
finding: Meta-analysis of 51 studies from 1997-2003 using the Levin typology. Risky-choice framing is a moderate effect, larger than attribute framing. Effects vary a lot between studies.
numbers: 151 effect sizes, about 13,500 subjects. d = 0.437 risky, 0.260 attribute, 0.444 goal. Risky framing k=87 (Q(86)=492.5, p<.0001). Asian disease problem was 47.7% of all tasks, d = 0.43. Design: between-subjects d=0.50 (k=72) vs within-subjects d=0.18 (k=15). Students d=0.44. More women in sample gave larger effect (R2=0.191, p<.001). More options gave smaller effect (beta=-0.40, p=.046). Product tasks d=0.89, k=4.
limits: Only studies from 1997-2003. 83% student samples, 89% between-subjects. Few unpublished studies, so publication bias is possible. Heterogeneity is large, so one pooled d hides much.
agent_relevance: A realistic prior for how a wording shift moves a decision: moderate, not a flip. Seeing both wordings within one subject cuts the effect by about two thirds, which supports showing the agent the second wording.

source: Zhou, Liu, Liao & Li (2021) Risky choice framing with various problem descriptions: a replication and extension study (JDM 16(2))
finding: Large preregistered replication of Kuhberger and Tanner (2010). Removing the stated zero outcome from the risky option removes the framing effect; removing the non-zero outcome roughly doubles it. This favours fuzzy-trace theory over prospect theory.
numbers: Study 1: 1,119 valid Chinese participants (about 186 per cell). Classic task: 44.05% risky in gain vs 64.71% in loss, F(1,1113)=37.55, eta2p=.033. Zero complement removed: 57.22% vs 53.63%, F=1.14, p=.286 (no effect). Non-zero complement removed: 30.65% gain vs 76.46% loss, F=185.80, eta2p=.143. Interaction eta2p=.088. Original (N=558): 30/61%, ns, 23/78%. Studies 2 and 3 (N=892 and 906) varied risky probability 25/47/72% and expected value.
limits: Chinese online samples. Hypothetical child-health scenarios, not the exact Asian disease text. Original used US, German and other European participants.
agent_relevance: What counts is the structure of the options, not the words gain or loss. Our S1 rewrite should state every outcome explicitly as both complements, because a missing zero outcome removes or inflates the effect.

source: Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn (2015) Data Colada [11]: Mandel exactly-wording replication
finding: Mandel (2014) claimed the Asian disease effect comes from reading 'save 200' as 'at least 200', and that adding 'exactly' removes it. A larger replication found the effect stays with 'exactly'.
numbers: Original T&K 1981: 72% chose sure option in gain frame, 22% in loss frame. Mandel study 2 (about 38 per cell): original wording 58% vs 26%; with 'exactly' 59% vs 43% (drop not significant, p=.293). Data Colada replication (about 98 per cell, 2.5 times larger, mTurk): strong effect with 'exactly', p<.001. Simonsohn class data, 'exactly' wording, N=250: 63% vs 25%.
limits: Blog report, not peer reviewed. Percentages for the replication itself are in a figure not given in text. Mandel replied separately and disputes the reading.
agent_relevance: Making numbers precise ('exactly', 'at least') is not enough alone to neutralise a frame. A full canonical restatement is safer than clarifying wording.

source: Mandel & Kapler (2018) Cognitive style and frame susceptibility in decision-making (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Cognitive style does not predict who shows the framing effect. CRT, numeracy, actively open-minded thinking and need for cognition explained almost nothing of frame-consistent choice.
numbers: Exp 1: 190 students; frame-consistent 75% in positive frame, 49% in negative, 62% overall. Exp 2: 316 mTurk workers; 65% and 52%, 58.2% overall. Pooled N=506, correlations with frame-consistent choice r = 0.02 to 0.08, all not significant. CRT zero-order r=.16 in Exp 1, gone after controlling frame. Both experiments used 'exactly' wording.
limits: Between-subjects, one Asian disease isomorph. Null results for individual differences do not show the effect is the same size for everyone. Cognitive style measures are noisy.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a smarter or more careful model to be immune. Capability alone is not a defence; a structural step (second wording) is needed.

source: Klein et al. (2014, 2018) Many Labs 1 and 2, gain-loss framing, via FORRT replication atlas
finding: Many Labs 1 replicated the Asian disease gain-loss effect in a large multi-site test. Many Labs 2 replicated it again with a smaller effect.
numbers: Many Labs 1: d = 0.60, chi2(1)=516.41, p<.0001 (36 labs; a secondary blog says 31 of 36 labs significant). Many Labs 2 (2018): d = 0.40, 95% CI [0.35, 0.45], OR = 2.06 [1.87, 2.27], aggregate N = 7,228; described as less than half the original size.
limits: Page is a secondary summary table, I did not open the original papers. Total N for Many Labs 1 not given on the page. The 31 of 36 figure is from a non-peer-reviewed blog.
agent_relevance: The effect is robust at scale but shrinks from the original: plan for a moderate effect, about d 0.4 to 0.6 in humans.

source: Rachev et al. (2021) Replicating the Disease framing problem during the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic (PLOS ONE)
finding: Largest cross-national test of the Asian disease problem: 47 countries. The effect replicated in aggregate but varied by country. Stress and concern about the disease increased it.
numbers: N = 88,181 from 47 countries, between-subjects. Overall log-odds B=1.24 (SE .04), d = .69 (Many Labs reference d = .60). US d=.75 vs .63 in Many Labs. Frame x country chi2(46)=314.51, p<.001. Stress x frame B=.03, p=.03, BF=256.7; coronavirus concern x frame B=.05, p<.001, BF=124. Trust in government x frame not significant (p=.16).
limits: Only the first 100,000 characters of the page were read, per-country tables are in supplements. Online convenience samples, collected March-May 2020.
agent_relevance: Emotionally loaded context strengthens the effect. If a task statement carries alarm or stakes language, strip it in the neutral rewrite.

source: Best & Charness (2015) Age differences in the effect of framing on risky choice: a meta-analysis (Psychology and Aging)
finding: Age moderates risky-choice framing only in the gain frame and only for some content. Younger adults chose the risky option more in gain frames, mainly for lives and larger stakes.
numbers: 18 studies, 3,232 participants, 51 effect sizes (Hedges g, positive = older riskier). Gain frame: g=-0.25 [-0.33,-0.18], I2=86%. Loss frame: g=-0.02 [-0.10,0.06], ns. Gain frame, large mortality: g=-0.96 [-1.26,-0.65]; small financial g=-0.40; large financial g=-0.04 ns. Loss frame large mortality g=-1.35 on only 2 effect sizes.
limits: Very high heterogeneity (I2 86-93%). Small k in several subgroups. Egger tests ns, no p-curve.
agent_relevance: Domain matters: lives-at-stake wording is the strongest trigger. Treat medical or safety tasks as highest risk for frame effects.

source: Broniatowski & Reyna (2018) A formal model of fuzzy-trace theory: variations on framing effects and the Allais paradox (Decision)
finding: A formal fuzzy-trace model fitted to 88 published framing replications. It predicted most gain-loss pairs, including cases where prospect theory has no account (e.g. missing outcomes).
numbers: 88 gain-loss pairs: model predicted 82 (93%). 153 of 170 eligible conditions fit (90%). Asian disease between-subjects: 27 replications, predicted log-odds differed from reported in 1 (4%). 36 of 39 standard Asian disease experiments matched (92%). Within-subjects framing: 2 of 3 predicted. Low-PISA countries showed stronger effects, t(30)=2.06, p=.048. Within-subjects parameters smaller than between, t(15)=2.84, p=.01.
limits: Authors are fuzzy-trace proponents. Model has free parameters fit to data. Only the first 100,000 of about 278,000 characters were read.
agent_relevance: Supports a gist account: the model reads 'some saved vs none saved' as a categorical contrast. Writing options in the same gist (both complements shown) is a principled fix.

source: Peters & Levin (2008) Dissecting the risky-choice framing effect: numeracy as an individual-difference factor (JDM 3(6))
finding: Numeracy changes how the frame acts. Low-numeracy people show a frame effect beyond their ratings of each option. High-numeracy choices are almost fully explained by their option ratings.
numbers: N=108 students (positive frame n=53, negative n=55), five Asian disease variants, median split on numeracy (n=52 low, 56 high). Frame by numeracy interaction F(1,104)=3.9, p=.05 on choice. Framing significant for the less numerate (p<.001), not for the highly numerate.
limits: Median split, modest N, student sample. Earlier work cited in the paper found numeracy did not moderate risky-choice framing, so this is a contested moderator. Mandel & Kapler (2018) found no numeracy effect.
agent_relevance: Mixed evidence that number skill protects. If it does, it acts by integrating all numbers, which is what a canonical restatement does mechanically.

source: Nakamura (2016) Our morals really depends on our language: the foreign language effect within participants (CogSci)
finding: The 'foreign language effect' on framing (weaker effect in a second language, Keysar et al. 2012) was only partly replicated within subjects. It reduced the framing gap for a financial-crisis problem but not for the Asian disease problem.
numbers: N=132 Japanese undergraduates, each answering in native and foreign language. Foreign language reduced the gain-loss gap in the Financial crisis problem; no significant difference in the Asian disease problem. Coherence (same option across both frames) did not differ between languages in either problem. Keysar et al. 2012 reported, in the native condition, 77% sure option in gain vs 47% in loss (via secondary source).
limits: Short conference paper; exact percentages are in figures. The Keysar numbers are second-hand. A later study (cited in a search summary) found no reduction in a foreign language.
agent_relevance: Translating or rephrasing is not a reliable debiaser for this classic problem. Do not count on a language switch.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of large language models via human cognitive biases
finding: GPT-3 reproduced the Asian disease direction: it chose the risky option far more under the 'die' wording than the 'save' wording, near the original probability (1/3). At higher save probabilities both wordings gave mostly risky choices.
numbers: Probability of choosing the risky option, averaged over save probability ranges: save framing 11.3% (p<0.5), 21.9% (p=0.5), 84.4% (p>0.5), 45.4% overall. Die framing 60.0%, 46.9%, 93.8%, 74.1% overall. Tversky and Kahneman 1981 humans: 28% (save) vs 78% (die). Prompt used 600 people, 'Exactly 400 people will die' wording.
limits: GPT-3 (2022, older model). The probability and population varied, so only the 1/3 regime matches humans. The Asian disease text is probably in training data.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that LLMs inherit the direction of the human effect. The gap is large, so the same prompt in two wordings is a cheap test.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee & Nguyen (2023) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT rated a drug more effective when told '70 of 100 improved' than '30 of 100 did not improve', matching humans. The authors deliberately avoided the classic Asian disease text.
numbers: Study 3: ChatGPT gain frame rating 5 in all 11 trials, loss frame rating 4 in all 11 trials (1-7 scale). Humans (mTurk, N=82: 44 gain, 39 loss): 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86, p<.001.
limits: Attribute framing (efficacy rating), not risky choice. Only 11 trials per frame with no variance for ChatGPT, so no usable test statistic. Authors note ChatGPT refused to give choice answers.
agent_relevance: Even a rating (not a choice) shifts one full point on a 7-point scale from a pure wording change. Applies to any scoring step in the scaffold.

source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI decision under risk: prospect theory emerges in large language models
finding: Five frontier models, including reasoning models, show gain-loss framing, but the size and even the sign depend on the scenario. Military and sporting contexts give huge effects; business is near zero; a career scenario reverses.
numbers: Models: o3, Claude-4, Claude-4-Thinking, GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro. Framing effect (loss minus gain risk score, 0-2 scale). Championship strategy: +1.40 to +1.84 (GPT-4o +1.84; BLITZ chosen 85.6% in loss vs 0.8% in gain). Career transition: -0.37 to -0.60 (reverse). Business merger: -0.24 to +0.12. Framing size was not significantly correlated with attempts at expected-value calculation. Three-option tasks, original scenarios.
limits: Single-author, small samples per cell (about 125 per cell shown), scenario design not validated. Options are not exactly equal in all semantic respects, so some 'frame' effect may be real content difference.
agent_relevance: The frame is not only gain or loss but the whole scenario language. Even thinking models and explicit EV calculation did not remove it.

source: Ge, Zhang & Vorobeychik (2026) Mind the (DH) gap! A contrast in risky choices between reasoning and conversational LLMs
finding: 20 LLMs sort into reasoning models and conversational models. Reasoning models are close to expected-value maximisers and ignore gain-loss framing, prospect order and explanation prompts. Conversational models are strongly affected by all three.
numbers: 20 frontier and open LLMs plus a matched human sample. Correlation of reasoning models with the expected-payoff reference: 0.86 to 1. Conversational models below 0.5. Highest LLM-human correlation 0.42 (Claude Haiku). Humans were less affected by framing than conversational models. Paired open-model comparisons point to training for mathematical reasoning as the key factor.
limits: Two-option money prospects, not the lives-saved Asian disease text. Exact per-model frame effect sizes are in figures, not read.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that a reasoning-trained model resists the frame. Our agent should still verify because the resistance is tied to explicit prospects, and the paper shows a description-versus-history gap.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Same probabilities, different advice: gain-loss framing effects in high-stakes LLM decision support (FrameBench-HPS)
finding: Framing the same probability as gain or loss changes the recommendation category in about a third of cases across seven LLMs. Almost all changes move to or from uncertainty, not outright reversals.
numbers: 2,880 prompts from 240 scenarios (healthcare, finance, education/career, legal), seven LLMs, temperature 0. Category change 32.41% [30.48, 34.36]; direct reversal 0.63%. By model: 63.33% (highest), GPT-5 33.40%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 32.56%, GPT-4.1-mini 29.17%, Gemini 3 Flash 23.38%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 22.81%, Qwen3-VL-235B 21.58%. Same-frame repeat disagreement 7.12%. Risk shift 0.535 at 20% outcome probability falling to 0.109 at 80%. Conversational paraphrase: 34.20% vs 36.81% original.
limits: Open-ended advice, not forced choice. Robustness subset used 32 held-out scenarios and three models. LLM-labelled structured fields plus a human check.
agent_relevance: Direct test of our S1 idea; see b16 for the fix. The framing effect is 4 to 5 times the same-frame noise floor of 7.12%.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) FrameBench-HPS interventions: canonicalization vs frame-robust prompting
finding: Rewriting inputs to show both complementary probabilities works much better than just telling the model to notice the complement.
numbers: Matched-repeat category change under conversational prompting 34.20%; canonicalization 6.68% (95% CI 5.12-8.51; paired drop 27.52 points, CI 24.13-30.82); frame-robust instruction 22.83%. Mean loss-minus-gain risk shift: baseline 0.363, canonicalization -0.010 [-0.032, 0.010], frame-robust 0.154. Confidence gap 0.477 to 0.145 (canonicalization) and 0.400 (frame-robust). Direct reversals 0.52% baseline, 0.35% canonicalization, 1.56% frame-robust.
limits: Three models, 32 scenarios, three repeats. Frame-robust prompting slightly raised direct reversals. Only tested for binary-probability prompts.
agent_relevance: Strongest quantitative support for a code-run input normalisation step: rewrite input to a frame-free form before the model reasons, landing near the 7.12% repeat-noise floor. An instruction to 'ignore the frame' is the weaker option.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley & He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster, Findings of EMNLP)
finding: With admit versus reject wording in a student-admissions task, GPT-4 admitted far more students under one framing. Letting the model rewrite the prompt to remove the biased parts (self-help) removed the framing gap for GPT-4, but not reliably for small models.
numbers: 16,800-prompt dataset. GPT-4 admit rate 0.375 (admit framing) vs 0.780 (reject framing), difference -0.405 baseline. GPT-3.5 baseline +0.165. With self-help rewrite: GPT-4 -0.010, GPT-3.5 -0.080. Self-help left 2.7% of biased framing prompts for GPT-4, 0% for Llama-2 13B, 1.4% for Llama-2 7B. Few-shot debiasing sometimes drove admission rate to 0 or 1 (instruction failure).
limits: Admissions task, not gambles, so not the Asian disease structure. Direction of the GPT-4 effect is opposite to GPT-3.5. Older models.
agent_relevance: Model-written neutral rewrite works for strong models. Pair it with a check that the rewritten prompt kept all facts and numbers.

source: Huang, Zhang, Kwak & An (2026) CogBias: measuring and mitigating cognitive bias in LLMs
finding: Prompt-level debiasing helps framing a little but backfires for other judgment biases. Activation steering reduces bias scores 26-32%.
numbers: Three models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B), greedy decoding. Framing effect accuracy 35.6% under biased prompt vs 41.4% with debias prompt (+5.8 points). Several judgment biases worsened with debiasing (down 21.0 points for one). Steering gave 26-32% lower bias score; Qwen lost up to 19.0 points on judgment benchmarks.
limits: Computable-baseline version of framing, not the human Asian disease paradigm. Prompt-only debiasing gain for framing is small (5.8 points).
agent_relevance: A generic 'be unbiased' instruction gives only a small gain on framing and can hurt other tasks. Do not rely on a global debias prompt.

source: Pilli & Nallur (2026) Predicting biased human decision-making with LLMs in conversational settings
finding: A preregistered human study found risky-choice framing grows after a mentally demanding chatbot dialogue (cognitive load). GPT-4 family predicted individual choices and reproduced the load-bias pattern best; GPT-5 and open models fit worse.
numbers: Human N = 1,648 total; framing study 548 valid after filtering (from 595). Cohen's h (best reading of a garbled table): risky-choice framing 0.205 [-0.001, 0.410] in simple dialogue (ns) and 0.730 [0.524, 0.937] in complex dialogue (p=.001). Original Wang study h=0.193. Attribute framing did not replicate strongly. Goal framing strong.
limits: Table layout in the extracted text was garbled, so the h values for risky-choice rows are the best reading, not certain. Hypothetical chatbot task. The LLM part tested prediction of humans, not the models' own framing.
agent_relevance: Context length and mental demand in the preceding text can amplify the frame in people. Whether long contexts do the same for the agent is a testable hypothesis, not shown here.

source: Wang & Zhang (2026) Framing effects in independent-agent LLMs: a cross-family behavioral analysis
finding: A threshold voting game in two logically close wordings produced a near total swing across 82 models in 11 families. Susceptibility varies by model lineage.
numbers: 82 models, 11 families, 20 independent trials per prompt. Option B chosen in 4.3% of trials under instrumental framing vs 68.8% under cooperative framing.
limits: Social dilemma wording, not gain-loss. The two wordings differ in more than valence (cooperative vs instrumental language), so it is not a clean equivalent-description test. Only the abstract, introduction and results lines were read.
agent_relevance: Wording can dominate choice in independent parallel agents, so any voting or ensemble of agents sharing one wording will share the same bias.

source: Tarabeih (2026) Prospect theory in LLMs: a meta-analysis of loss aversion, diminishing sensitivity and probability weighting
finding: Across 11 studies and 32 models, LLMs show modest loss aversion and near-linear value, but a human-like inverted-S probability weighting. So the gain-loss asymmetry is weaker in LLMs than in people.
numbers: 102 fitted estimates, 11 studies, 32 models. Pooled lambda = 1.26 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.46) vs human 1.96 (strongest) and 1.07 / 1.31 (conservative). Symmetric gains and losses: 1.15 vs 1.07 in humans; unequal: 1.46 vs 2.3. Value curvature 1.01 (Tversky-Kahneman method) vs human 0.67; 0.52 (Tanaka) vs 0.67. Probability weighting 0.81 and 0.84.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read for this entry. Few studies behind probability weighting. Results shift with model family and fitting method.
agent_relevance: Frame effects in LLMs are not simply human loss aversion. Look for them by testing, not by assuming the human pattern.

source: Kuhberger (1998) The influence of framing on risky decisions: a meta-analysis (OBHDP), figures as relayed by web summaries of Steiger & Kuhberger (2018)
finding: The first big meta-analysis found a small-to-moderate framing effect in risky choice. A later p-curve bias-correction reanalysis put it higher.
numbers: 1998: 136 studies, 230 effect sizes, about 30,000 participants, d = 0.31. Steiger & Kuhberger (2018) p-curve corrected d about 0.52; also d = 0.56 in a newer meta-analysis of 2016 studies (second-hand).
limits: Not opened: the publisher pages were blocked, numbers come from search summaries and a replication blog. Verify before quoting.
agent_relevance: Gives a range for the human effect: d 0.31 uncorrected, about 0.5 corrected.

source: Diederich, Wyszynski & Ritov (2018) Moderators of framing effects in variations of the Asian disease problem (JDM 13(6)); Guo et al. (2017, Psychological Science)
finding: Short decision time seems to increase the framing effect, which fits a fast-intuition account. This is opposite to an older finding by Svenson and Benson (1993).
numbers: No numbers verified. Search summary only: Svenson & Benson 1993 (40-second deadline) reduced framing; Diederich et al. 2018 and Guo et al. 2017 report amplification under time pressure; a 2021 preregistered replication (N=40) attributes this to attention and truncated search.
limits: Not opened: publisher sites blocked (403 or connection refused). Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: If true, giving a model a short token budget could raise frame sensitivity; test directly rather than assume.

source: Thomas & Millar (2012); Almashat et al. (2008); Garcia (2013); Akbulut (2015): debiasing interventions for framing (secondary web summary)
finding: Interventions that reduced framing in people: an analytic-goal instruction, listing pros and cons of each option, and icon-array visual formats. An explicit warning alone gave no steady reduction in one thesis.
numbers: No effect sizes verified. Reported only in search summaries: Almashat 2008 pros-and-cons task reduced framing; Garcia 2013 (60 senior police officers): no framing effect with icon arrays; Akbulut 2015: warnings and analytic processing, alone or combined, did not steadily decrease susceptibility.
limits: Not opened, no numbers. Thesis-level evidence for the warning result.
agent_relevance: Support for making the model write out both complements for each option (like the pros and cons task) rather than just warning it.

source: Mandel (2014) Do framing effects reveal irrational choice? (JEP: General), as relayed by Data Colada and Mandel & Kapler (2018)
finding: Rival to prospect theory and fuzzy-trace: people read 'save 200' as 'at least 200', so the two frames are not logically equivalent for them. In Mandel's data the effect appeared mainly among lower-bound readers.
numbers: Per Mandel & Kapler (2018, opened): framing effect appeared only for lower-bound readers; exact readers showed no significant effect. Per Data Colada (opened): the 'exactly' reduction was not significant in Mandel's own data (58/26 vs 59/43) and the larger replication kept the effect.
limits: The paper itself was blocked (403). Findings are second-hand from opened pages that cite it.
agent_relevance: Even if the frame is partly an underspecified number, the fix is the same for our agent: state exact complements.

source: Levin, Schneider & Gaeth (1998) All frames are not created equal: a typology and critical analysis of framing effects (OBHDP 76)
finding: Splits valence framing into risky-choice, attribute and goal framing, and argues contradictory results came from mixing them. Later meta-analyses adopted it.
numbers: Abstract only (search summary). Meta-analytic follow-up in Pinon & Gambara (opened): risky d=0.437, attribute 0.260, goal 0.444.
limits: Not opened as full text. Only the abstract reached me through search.
agent_relevance: Our S1 check should name the frame type: option-structure frames (risky choice) behave differently from attribute labels ('70% survive' vs '30% die').
